title: The Invisible Man: A Grotesque Romance
description: Published in 1897: the story of Griffin, a scientist who makes himself invisible and is destroyed by the consequences of his own discovery. It is a prose fiction work of 1897 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale.
plot_or_argument: Griffin takes refuge in the village of Iping, robs and terrorises the neighbourhood, takes shelter with Dr Kemp and reveals his plan for a reign of terror, and is hunted and killed by the mob in Port Burdock.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
principal_characters: Griffin; Doctor Kemp; Mrs Hall; Mr Marvel; Doctor Cuss; Colonel Adye
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the single scientific premise developed to its consequences.
historical_context: The 1890s, the physics of light and refraction, the new research university, and the English fear of the unregulated scientist. The record dates the work as composed in 1897 and first published in 1897 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
literary_significance: The Invisible Man is the classic English fable of the scientist without a moral community: its subject is not invisibility but the isolation and violence it produces, and it founded the modern literature of the dangerous discovery.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. G. Wells. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in Pearson's Weekly from June to December 1897 and published by C. Arthur Pearson in November 1897; the full title is The Invisible Man: A Grotesque Romance. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Island of Doctor Moreau
description: Published in 1896 and the most disturbing of Wells's early romances: the story of a shipwrecked man who finds on a Pacific island a physiologist who turns animals into human beings. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Edward Prendick is rescued by the schooner Ipecacuanha, is put ashore on Moreau's island, and discovers that the vivisectionist is creating the Beast Folk, who live under a Law spoken by Moreau and his assistant Montgomery; Moreau is killed by a puma-woman, Montgomery dies, and Prendick returns to England to a horror of his own species.
narrative_structure: A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
principal_characters: Edward Prendick; Doctor Moreau; Montgomery; the Beast Folk; M'ling; the Sayer of the Law
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the single scientific premise developed to its consequences.
historical_context: The 1890s, the anti-vivisection movement, the Darwinian account of the continuity of species, and the imperial logic of the colonial laboratory. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; naturalist and determinist novel.
literary_significance: The Island of Doctor Moreau is the central English text on vivisection, evolution and the fear of the animal within; its images of the Law, the Beast Folk and the return to the beast made it a permanent point of reference for posthumanist criticism.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. G. Wells. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

title: The Wheels of Chance: A Bicycling Idyll
alternative_titles: Wheels of Chance: A Bicycling Idyll
description: Published in 1896 and the most charming of the early Wells novels: the story of a draper's assistant on a bicycling holiday who rescues a young woman from a predatory novelist, and learns that romance belongs to a class he cannot enter.
plot_or_argument: Hoopdriver, a draper's assistant, sets off on a bicycle tour of the south of England, meets Jessie Milton, rescues her from the pursuit of Bechamel, rides with her to the coast, and returns to his shop after a brief and poignant adventure.
narrative_structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
principal_characters: Mr Hoopdriver, the draper's assistant; Jessie Milton; Bechamel; Mrs Milton ('Thomas Plantagenet'), Jessie's stepmother; Phipps; Widgery; Dangle
literary_form: Novel; realist novel of common life
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the single scientific premise developed to its consequences.
historical_context: The 1890s, the bicycle craze, the new leisure of the working man, the drapery trade, and the beginnings of the 'New Woman' on wheels. The record dates the work as composed in 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; new woman and marriage-question novel.
literary_significance: The Wheels of Chance is the finest English novel of the bicycle and one of the first to record the democratisation of travel by the new machine; its class comedy makes it a key text of the 1890s.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. G. Wells. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

title: Kipps: The Story of a Simple Soul
description: Published in 1905 and the first of Wells's great comic novels of class: the story of Arthur Kipps, draper's assistant, who inherits a fortune and discovers that money cannot buy the manners, taste or confidence of the English middle class.
plot_or_argument: Kipps inherits a legacy and is propelled into the genteel leisure class he cannot inhabit; he is humiliated at a literary society, lost among builders and servants, and finally rescued by his marriage to his childhood sweetheart Ann, and the novel ends with the small happiness of a man who has stopped trying to be something else.
narrative_structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Arthur Kipps; Ann Pornick; Helen Walsingham; Chester Coote; Chitterlow; Mrs Walsingham; young Walsingham; Sid Pornick; Masterman; Mr Shalford
literary_form: Novel; realist novel of common life
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the single scientific premise developed to its consequences.
historical_context: The 1900s, the English class system in the decade of the great estates and the new professional classes, and Wells's own youthful apprenticeship in drapery. The record dates the work as composed between 1904 and 1905 and first published in 1905 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.

bibliographical_notes: Published by Macmillan in October 1905; the full title is Kipps: The Story of a Simple Soul. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Nature (1836)
description: Published anonymously in 1836 and the founding document of American Transcendentalism: a short book arguing that nature is the visible manifestation of spirit and that the individual may know God directly through it.
plot_or_argument: Emerson divides the essay into Nature, Commodity, Beauty, Language, Discipline, Idealism, Spirit and Prospects, and argues in each that the natural world is a symbol of the mind's own laws and that 'the kingdom of man over nature' is available to anyone who will look with fresh eyes.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work was published anonymously or under an initial, and the authorship was established afterwards.
historical_context: The 1830s, the American Unitarian crisis, the German idealism of Kant and Coleridge, and the new science of natural history. The record dates the work as composed between 1835 and 1836 and first published in 1836 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.

title: 'The American Scholar'
description: Delivered at Harvard on 31 August 1837 and published the same year: the address Oliver Wendell Holmes called 'our intellectual Declaration of Independence'. It is a prose work of 1837 by Ralph Waldo Emerson; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Lecture and Popular Address; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Emerson argues that the American scholar must draw his education from nature, from books and from action, and that the true scholar is 'Man Thinking'; he attacks the bookworm, the parrot of other men's thinking, and calls for an original American literature.
narrative_structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered.

The record dates the work as composed in 1837 and first published in 1837 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.

title: Divinity School Address
description: Delivered on 15 July 1838 and the most controversial religious address in American history: an attack on the historical Christianity of the churches in the name of the soul's immediate access to God. It is a prose work of 1838 by Ralph Waldo Emerson; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Lecture and Popular Address; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Emerson tells the graduating ministers that the church has made Jesus a historical idol, that the miracles and the scriptures have replaced the inward revelation, and that the preacher must speak from his own experience of the divine or not at all.
narrative_structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered.

The record dates the work as composed in 1838 and first published in 1838 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.

attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Waldo Emerson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1838, as address (harvard divinity school), by Ralph Waldo Emerson. Composed in 1838. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: 'Self-Reliance'
description: Published in Essays: First Series in 1841 and the most influential essay in American literature: the argument that the individual must trust his own thought against the whole weight of society, custom and history.
plot_or_argument: Emerson denounces conformity, consistency, philanthropy and travel as escapes from the self, and insists that 'whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist'; the essay builds an ethic of self-trust from the doctrine that the soul in each person is the same universal soul.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class.
historical_context: The 1840, the American democratic experiment, the reform movements of the 1840s, and the Romantic philosophy of the self. The record dates the work as composed between 1839 and 1841 and first published in 1841 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: 'Self-Reliance' is the central statement of American individualism and one of the most quoted essays in the language: it has shaped American ideas of the self, of originality and of dissent from Emerson's own day to the present.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Waldo Emerson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1841, as essay (in essays: first series), by Ralph Waldo Emerson. Composed between 1839 and 1841. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Representative Men
description: Published in 1850 and the fullest statement of Emerson's theory of great men: studies of Plato, Swedenborg, Montaigne, Shakespeare, Napoleon and Goethe. It is a prose work of 1850 by Ralph Waldo Emerson; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Emerson argues that each great man is a 'representative' of a faculty or an idea — the philosopher, the mystic, the sceptic, the poet, the man of the world, the writer — and that the study of great persons is the study of what the age needed and produced.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address.
historical_context: The 1840s, the American lecture circuit, the Carlylean cult of the hero, and the democratic objection to hero-worship. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1850 and first published in 1850 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: Representative Men is the central American statement of the philosophy of great men and a key text in the American reception of European culture; its essays on Montaigne and Shakespeare are among the best short criticism of the century.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Waldo Emerson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Phillips, Sampson in Boston in January 1850, from the lectures delivered in 1845-46 and revised after the English tour. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: English Traits
description: Published in 1856 and the most acute American book on England: a series of chapters on the English race, land, aristocracy, universities, religion, literature and character, drawn from three visits. It is a prose work of 1856 by Ralph Waldo Emerson; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Emerson describes the English as a nation of shopkeepers with an instinct for the sea, a genius for the practical, and a brutal class system; his portraits of the aristocracy, the Toryism of the English mind and the English Sunday are comic, exact and unsentimental.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
principal_characters: Ralph Waldo Emerson, the narrator; Coleridge, Wordsworth, Landor and Carlyle, whom he visits
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class.
historical_context: The 1850s, the Anglo-American literary relations of the period, the Great Exhibition of 1851, and the American debate on English institutions. The record dates the work as composed between 1847 and 1856 and first published in 1856 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
literary_significance: English Traits is the best portrait of the English national character by an American and a key text in the literature of national character; it shaped the American image of England for a generation.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Waldo Emerson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1856, as travel book and national portrait, by Ralph Waldo Emerson. Composed between 1847 and 1856. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
description: Published in 1854 after nine years of revision and the central text of American nature writing: the account of two years, two months and two days in a cabin at Walden Pond, and of an experiment in living deliberately.
plot_or_argument: Thoreau describes the building of the house, the economy of his life, the reading of the classics, the sounds and visitors of the woods, the bean field, the pond, the animals, the seasons and the spring thaw, and ends with the parable of the artist of Kouroo.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
principal_characters: Henry David Thoreau, the narrator; Alek Therien, the woodchopper; John Field, the Irish labourer
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is concrete, comma-heavy cumulative sentences.
historical_context: The 1845-47, Concord and the Transcendentalist circle, the Mexican War and the market revolution, and the American debate on labour and simplicity. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1854 and first published in 1854 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: Walden is the founding text of American nature writing and one of the great works of American prose: it is at once a manual of economy, a naturalist's journal, a spiritual autobiography and a political argument, and it has shaped the modern environmental movement more than any other book.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as David Henry Thoreau. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Ticknor and Fields in Boston on 9 August 1854; seven editions were issued in the author's lifetime, each with revision, and the 1897 Riverside edition carries the pagination now standard. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: 'Resistance to Civil Government' ('Civil Disobedience')
description: Published in Aesthetic Papers in 1849 after Thoreau's night in the Concord jail in 1846: the founding modern argument for the primacy of individual conscience over the state. It is a prose work of 1849 by Henry David Thoreau; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Thoreau argues that a government that permits slavery and wages an unjust war forfeits the citizen's obedience; he describes his refusal to pay the poll tax, his imprisonment, and the principle that the individual must withdraw cooperation from injustice even at the cost of punishment.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.

The record dates the work as composed between 1848 and 1849 and first published in 1849 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.

attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as David Henry Thoreau. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1849, as political essay (aesthetic papers, 1849), by Henry David Thoreau. Composed between 1848 and 1849. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers

It is a prose work of 1849 by Henry David Thoreau; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Nature Essay and the Rural Observation and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.

narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence.

The record dates the work as composed between 1839 and 1849 and first published in 1849 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; nature essay and the rural observation.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1849, as travel narrative and essay, by Henry David Thoreau. Composed between 1839 and 1849. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: 'Slavery in Massachusetts'

It is a prose work of 1854 by Henry David Thoreau; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Lecture and Popular Address; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Thoreau attacks the state of Massachusetts for returning Burns, charges the press and the churches with complicity, and declares that the abolitionist must act against the government rather than petition it.

An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

title: 'Walking'

It is a prose work of 1862 by Henry David Thoreau; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Nature Essay and the Rural Observation and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
